newsitem.title: UK: Doubts on Italy in EMU 1999 need not affect Spain.
newsitem.headline: Doubts on Italy in EMU 1999 need not affect Spain.

text.p: Doubts Italy will make it to the single currency starting line intensified on Wednesday but analysts say this should not prevent fellow southern Europeans Spain and Portugal from joining in 1999.

Italy's aspirations to join European monetary union (EMU) in 1999 were dealt a fresh blow on Wednesday following reports that a compromise plan to allow Italy to join the single currency after 1999 was being considered by European Central bankers and monetary officials.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi angrily rejected the idea, saying Rome was "solemnly committed" to meeting membership terms for EMU at the outset, while officials in France and Germany denied knowledge of such a plan.

But the reports, which pushed the lira down to a two-month lows of 992.50 lire against the mark, raised doubts in some quarters that the other so-called "Club Med" nations Spain and Portugal would also be left in the cold.
The political implications of Spain and Portugal joining EMU at the outset without Italy - the only Club Med nation with G7 status and EU founding member to boot - are clear, say some.

"If they (Italians) are left out, it would be a serious blow - just remember Italy was one of the first countries in the European Community - and it may well provoke a feeling of 'well do we want all this?'," said Elizabeth Legge, economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin.
But analysts on Wednesday said it is economics which in the end will define if Spain and Portugal join at the outset and Italy does not.

"Ultimately, it comes down to economic fundamentals. Spain and Portugal will be able to meet the criteria, and as long as they are judged on the Maastricht criteria that has been laid out, they will be accepted," said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi International.
"Italy will will come closer than people think, but I don't think they will meet the Maastricht criteria," she said.
Italy's debt numbers are horrendous, say analysts. The Maastricht treaty states that total debt should account for no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Forecasts for Italy's 1996 debt numbers are forecast at 121.3 percent of GDP and at 121.7 percent of GDP for 1997. "That is huge," said one analyst.
For Portugal and Spain, the numbers are smaller. Spain has forecast 1997 debt-to-GDP at 69.3 percent and Portugal at 69.9 percent.

Analysts also say Italy also risks GDP growth coming in lower than forecasts of 1.5 percent for 1997 and that Eurostat, the European statistics body, may not accept certain Italian accounting principles.
Strict interpretation of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) criteria, say analysts, could also exclude Italy since a country needs to be in the ERM two years prior to the decision on the EMU is taken.
Italy re-joined the ERM in November of 1996, while the Portuguese joined in April 1992 and Spain in 1989.
"There are various loopholes that can be used if they are determined to keep Italy out," said a European economist.
Only by limiting EMU at first to countries with hard currencies can the euro hope to win the market's confidence, German government officials and bankers have said.
"The price to be paid for a single currency will be the exclusion of the lira - temporarily - for 12 months," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.

Financial markets, which have been betting on Italy being in monetary union at the launch on January 1, 1999 could be appeased even if the date is missed - provided, say analysts, it is clear they would form part of a second wave of entrants.
"Providing Italy is in by 2002, I don't think they would be too upset," said Yamaichi's Brickman.
Analysts say Germany is against having Italy in at EMU's outset because it would make it harder to persuade Germans to give up the mark and could weigh on the euro from the start.

"There is fear within the electorate (German) that Italy is not a stable country in terms of politics and fiscal policy," said Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust. "That they (Germans) have to give up the D-mark for a more inflation-prone currency is definitely not a palatable choice".
The size of Italy's economy, and concern by some it cannot maintain post-EMU fiscal success are also concerns.
"The real problem is that the Italian economy is bigger...And the Germans do not want to get involved in supporting the Italian economy. I think that is going to be the problem," said Legge.
